title: What C Is and How It Runs
relevance: SDE interviews use this to check whether candidates understand how C becomes a binary, what linking and the ABI imply, and why undefined behavior is not just a crash.

phases.goal: Establish what C is for, how its standards evolved, and the meaning of a minimal hosted program.

must_hit.point: C is a small, fast, close-to-the-hardware systems language designed in the early 1970s by Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs to write Unix, with minimal abstraction and full trust in the programmer.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions systems/Unix origins, closeness to hardware, and that C trusts the programmer rather than hiding the machine.

must_hit.point: C standards progressed from informal K&R C through ANSI C (C89/C90) to C99, C11, C17, and C23; the chosen -std= flag controls which language features and library functions are available.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists the major standard lineage and ties the compiler -std flag to feature/library availability.

must_hit.point: In a hosted program, int main(void) is the entry point; printf writes to stdout; return 0; ends the process with exit status 0 meaning success by convention; every C program has stdin, stdout, and stderr.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks Hello World pieces: main signature, stdout printing, exit status 0, and the three standard streams.

probes: What standard of C do you typically target, and why does it matter?
Walk through what each line of a Hello World C program does, including return 0.

hints.1: Think about where C still dominates and why a language that close to the machine would have evolving ISO standards.
hints.2: Separate philosophy (hardware/Unix), the K&R→C89/C90→C99→C11→C17→C23 line, and the roles of #include, main, printf, and exit status.
hints.3: Say C was built for Unix with minimal abstraction; standards from K&R through C23 matter because -std selects features; main returns int, 0 means success, and stdin/stdout/stderr are the three default streams.

phases.goal: Establish the translation pipeline, translation units/object files, and the abstract-machine behavior categories including ABI binding.

must_hit.point: gcc as a driver runs four stages in order: preprocessing (strip comments, expand macros, paste #include text), compilation to architecture-specific assembly, assembly into an object file of raw machine code, then linking that resolves external references (e.g. printf) into a final executable.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names all four stages and distinguishes text expansion, assembly text, object binary, and linker resolution of externals.

must_hit.point: A translation unit is one .c file after the preprocessor has expanded macros and pasted includes; an object file (.o/.obj) holds that unit's machine code but is not yet executable until the linker connects unresolved references.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defines translation unit vs object file and says linking is what makes an executable.

must_hit.point: The C standard describes an Abstract Machine and splits behavior into well-defined, implementation-defined (compiler chooses and documents), unspecified (compiler may choose without documenting), and undefined behavior (no requirements once rules are violated).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names the abstract machine and all four behavior buckets with the documentation distinction for implementation-defined vs unspecified.

must_hit.point: Compiled C is native code bound to a CPU architecture and OS via an ABI that contracts memory layout and which registers pass function arguments; targeting another machine requires cross-compilation for that ABI.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Ties native binary to architecture/OS, defines ABI (layout and argument registers), and mentions cross-compiling.

probes: What happens between typing gcc main.c -o myprogram and getting a runnable binary?
What is a translation unit, and how is it different from an object file?
What are the four categories of behavior in the C standard?

hints.1: Picture an assembly line from source text to a binary, then ask what rules the standard actually guarantees.
hints.2: Order preprocess → compile to assembly → assemble to .o → link; define TU and object file; list well-defined, implementation-defined, unspecified, and UB; mention ABI.
hints.3: Preprocessor pastes/expands into a translation unit; compiler emits assembly; assembler emits .o; linker resolves printf and builds the executable; behavior is one of four buckets on the abstract machine; the binary must match the target ABI.

phases.goal: Establish the performance/portability and standard-compatibility tradeoffs the material calls out.

must_hit.point: Unlike Python or JavaScript, C compiles to native code the CPU runs directly: maximum performance and minimal overhead, at the cost of portability because the binary is tied to architecture and OS.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the native-code performance win and the portability cost of architecture/OS binding.

must_hit.point: Teams often target C11 or C17 for broad compatibility while treating C99 as a baseline (e.g. stdint.h, inline declarations); newer features such as C99 variable-length arrays (optional in C11) may be missing on legacy or specialized embedded compilers.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions C11/C17 vs C99 baseline and that VLAs or similar newer features may not exist on embedded/legacy toolchains.

probes: Why does compiling to native code help and hurt compared with an interpreted language?
Why does the C standard you target matter on embedded or legacy compilers?

hints.1: Compare who executes the program—the CPU directly vs a runtime—and who must support your chosen language dialect.
hints.2: Native binary: speed/overhead vs portability; standard choice: C11/C17 compatibility vs C99 features that optional/embedded compilers may omit.
hints.3: Say native code gives max performance/minimal overhead but binds you to ABI/architecture; say C11/C17 for compatibility, C99 baseline for stdint.h/inlines, and VLAs optional in C11 may fail on embedded compilers.

phases.goal: Establish practical compiler flags, stage-stopping switches, and what a running process's memory regions are.

must_hit.point: A robust baseline compile is gcc -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -O2 -g: select C17, enable broad warnings, moderate optimization, and embed debug info mapping machine code back to source lines.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Recalls the flag set and what -std, -Wall/-Wextra, -O2, and -g each do.

must_hit.point: Stop the pipeline to inspect artifacts with -E (preprocessed text), -S (assembly, e.g. main.s), and -c (object file, e.g. main.o); linking object files with the C library produces the executable.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Maps -E/-S/-c to preprocessed source, .s assembly, and .o object, then linking to the final binary.

must_hit.point: When the OS loader runs the binary it creates a process with Code (Text) for instructions, Data/BSS for globals/statics, Stack for locals and call bookkeeping, and Heap for dynamic runtime requests.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists Text/Code, Data/BSS, Stack, and Heap with their roles.

probes: Give a solid gcc command for a production-ish debug build and explain each flag.
How would you inspect preprocessed output, assembly, and an object file for hello.c before linking?
What memory regions exist in a process after the loader runs your binary?

hints.1: Think flags you always want on, then flags that stop early so you can read intermediates.
hints.2: Bundle -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -O2 -g; use -E/-S/-c for .i text, .s, and .o; name Text, Data/BSS, Stack, Heap after load.
hints.3: Quote the baseline gcc line; say -E shows expanded headers, -S yields assembly like call puts, -c yields binary .o, then link against libc; process layout is Code/Text, Data/BSS, Stack, Heap.

tradeoffs.topic: Native compiled C vs interpreted languages
tradeoffs.strong_answer: C compiles to native machine instructions the CPU executes directly, buying maximum performance and minimal overhead, but the binary is tightly bound to a target CPU architecture and OS, so portability requires recompilation or cross-compilation for the target ABI.

tradeoffs.topic: Newer C standard features vs legacy/embedded compiler support
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Targeting C11 or C17 favors broad compatibility, with C99 as a practical baseline for facilities like stdint.h and inline declarations; features such as C99 variable-length arrays—made optional in C11—may be unavailable on legacy or specialized embedded compilers, so the chosen -std matters for what you can rely on.

gotchas.trap: Treating #include like a Python-style module import.
gotchas.correction: #include is literal text inclusion: the preprocessor pastes the header into the source, so a massive header is fully processed every time that file is compiled.

gotchas.trap: Assuming a program that declares a function but never defines it will fail at compile time.
gotchas.correction: Syntax can still compile; the linker fails later with an undefined reference if the defining .c was never compiled/linked in.

gotchas.trap: Believing undefined behavior just means the program crashes or returns garbage.
gotchas.correction: UB means the standard imposes no requirements: the compiler may assume the invalid path never happens and may delete checks, break earlier code, or do anything else—never rely on it.
